messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kamal had always taken pride in his independence and self-reliance. As an auditor, he was meticulous and detail-oriented, able to navigate complex financial records with ease. But all of that changed on a night out with friends at a local club. It started like any other night - laughter, music, and dancing - but ended in a bathroom stall, where Kamal was brutally raped by a stranger. The smell of cheap cologne still made his stomach turn, transporting him back to that moment of utter helplessness. He would catch whiffs of it on the street, in elevators, or at parties, and suddenly he'd be frozen in time, reliving the terror. People misbehaving - whether it was someone cutting in line or honking aggressively in traffic - also triggered a visceral response in Kamal. He saw the world as a chaotic, unpredictable place where anyone could become a predator. Kamal's relationships suffered as well. When people made casual references to his ex, he felt like he'd been punched in the gut. It was as if they were taunting him, reminding him of his own vulnerability. His friends and family noticed the change in him - the constant looking over his shoulder, the quick exits from social gatherings - but Kamal couldn't explain it to them. In an effort to regain some sense of control, Kamal started taking certain precautions. He always made sure to stay close to an exit, whether he was at a restaurant or a friend's house. This way, he could make a swift escape if needed. Situations where others evaluated him - his appearance, his performance, his worth - became unbearable. Job reviews with his boss left him sweaty and anxious; even compliments from strangers made him cringe. Kamal started wearing loose-fitting clothes to avoid drawing attention to himself. Baggy shirts and jeans became his armor, protecting him from the prying eyes of others. He felt like a ghost hovering on the periphery of social interactions, invisible but constantly vigilant. The world had become a minefield for Kamal, full of potential threats waiting to be triggered. Unfamiliar places made him anxious - how could he assess the danger if he didn't know the layout? Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard; a friend's playful tap on the shoulder would send his heart racing. Kamal felt like his body was constantly on high alert, tense and ready to react to any perceived threat. His muscles ached from being coiled for so long, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Self-doubt crept in, too. Kamal couldn't shake the feeling that someone else - anyone else - would have avoided getting into this situation. He replayed the night of the assault over and over in his head, wondering what he could've done differently. He used to be a happy person, full of laughter and optimism, but now misery clung to him like a shroud. The sense of humiliation lingered, a festering wound that refused to heal. Kamal felt permanently tainted by the experience, as if he'd been branded with an invisible scar. His eyes would well up with tears when no one was looking, overwhelmed by the weight of his own shame. It took months for Kamal's loved ones to notice the toll this had taken on him. They staged an intervention, urging him to seek help before it was too late. What finally brought Kamal to therapy was a panic attack at work - he'd been reviewing financial records when a coworker approached him with a question, and suddenly he was back in that bathroom stall, fighting for air. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kamal knew what he wanted: to find a way out of this darkness, to rediscover the carefree person he once was. What he feared most was losing himself completely, becoming forever trapped in this prison of his own making.
